claims.text: Superconductivity in fully disordered, multi-element bcc HEAs is primarily governed by robust electron–phonon coupling and a stable density of states at the Fermi level.
Nb–Ta–Hf–Zr–Ti alloys have elements with similar atomic sizes and electronegativities.
Similarity in atomic size and electronegativity stabilizes the bcc structure in Nb–Ta–Hf–Zr–Ti HEAs.
The bcc alloy's electronic structure is resistant to lattice distortions and pressure.
Small composition shifts between Ti-rich and Nb–Ta-dominated fractions change valence electron count and local lattice distortions.
Composition-induced changes in valence electron count and local distortion tune Tc without causing a phase change.
(TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 has an ambient-pressure Tc of approximately 7.5–8 K.
The proposed starting alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase bcc solid solution.
The controlled intervention is to increase Ti or another constituent with a different valence electron count while retaining at least five elements at 5 at.% or more and preserving the bcc phase.
Arc melting or rapid quenching can preserve a single-phase disordered bcc structure and avoid phase segregation in the proposed samples.
Random atomic distribution in the bcc lattice produces a homogeneous electronic structure with stable Fermi-level density of states and robust electron–phonon coupling.
Configurational disorder averages local fluctuations in bonding and lattice strain.
Averaging of local bonding and strain fluctuations preserves the electronic structure and electron–phonon coupling that set Tc.
Increasing Ti within the single-phase bcc regime will produce a measurable shift in Tc while retaining robust superconductivity.
Tc and possibly Hc2 will vary systematically with composition.
The superconducting state of (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 persists to very high pressure.
The pressure robustness of the baseline is caused by its stable bcc structure.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase, disordered bcc solid solution.
Phase separation or formation of an ordered subphase will break the proposed relationship between composition, electronic structure, and superconductivity.
A lack of systematic correlation between composition or electronic density of states and superconducting behavior within the retained bcc phase would falsify the mechanism.
